paper_title: Selection-Based Structured Reasoning: Toward Efficient Multimodal Search Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multimodal agents commonly generate free-form reasoning before each action. For small models, limited model capacity can result in lengthy reasoning that provides little useful guidance for action generation while incurring substantial inference cost. To address this challenge, we introduce Selection-based Structured Reasoning (SSR), a framework that reformulates reasoning as selection instead of open-ended generation. SSR represents recurring high-level reasoning as pre-specified, reusable natural-language candidates. At each turn, the model selects from these reasoning candidates based on their likelihoods given the current context, without requiring an auxiliary task head. Using pre-specified reasoning traces enables parallel scoring, where teacher-forced prefilling computes token likelihoods concurrently within and across candidates using a shared context KV cache. We evaluate SSR on seven multimodal search benchmarks using 2B and 4B models. Across multiple reinforcement learning objectives and supervised fine-tuning, SSR delivers significant efficiency gains without sacrificing task performance. SSR achieves an average success rate competitive with leading search agents of the same scale, while reducing per-turn reasoning latency by over 90% and total per-question model inference latency by 28-54%. Project page: https://zfy0314.github.io/ssr-webpage/.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Multimodal agents turn textual and visual observations into actions: they analyze multimodal inputs, gather information, and use tools to resolve tasks that require multi-turn interactions (He et al., 2024; Chng et al., 2025). common agent design interleaves observations, freeform reasoning, and actions (Yao et al., 2022). The reasoning step lets the model assess the available evidence and decide what to do next, but adds sequential token generation cost before every action. For small, ondevice models with limited reasoning capacity, lengthy texts and repeated deliberations may waste the generation cost without providing useful guidance for generating better actions. An efficient agent needs reasoning that guides it to choose the desired action with minimal repeating cost of generating reasoning traces. Existing approaches reduce this overhead by prompting concise traces or rewarding shorter reasoning (Xu et al., 2025; Arora & Zanette, 2025). These approaches reduce the amount of text generated, yet keep the sequential dependency between its tokens during autoregressive decoding. We investigate an orthogonal direction: changing the representation of reasoning itself. We observed that in multimodal search, entities, queries, and observations vary across questions, but the high-level reasoning for taking the next action often recurs. For example, finding the location of an upcoming AI conference and the year LEGO was founded can share the same rationale: the entity is known but the requested information is missing, so search for the entity name and the attribute of interest. Previous work on thought templates (Yang et al., 2024; Ouyang et al., 2026) reported similar finding, showing the value of reusing reasoning knowledge across problems. Therefore, the required reasoning space for search agents does not span the entire natural language space. Instead, the model can achieve decent success rate with few reasoning candidates to choose from. Motivated by this, we introduce Selection-based Structured Reasoning (SSR), framework that formulates reasoning as selection among reusable natural-language candidates instead of openended freeform generation. At each turn, the agent selects reasoning candidate conditioned on its interaction history, then uses the selected reasoning to generate the next action and its arguments (e.g., text search with question-specific query). This design separates reusable reasoning patterns from instance-specific execution: the selected candidate provides the rationale for the next 1 Figure 1: SSR significantly reduces inference latency. Left: Parallel reasoning decoding replaces autoregressive reasoning generation. Right: Across four training objectives and two model sizes, SSR achieves comparable or higher success rates while reducing mean reasoning latency per turn by more than 90%. Mean total model inference latency per question is reduced by 2854%  (Table 2)  . step, while action generation supplies the details needed to realize it. The agent then adapts its actions to the current context without generating freeform reasoning traces at any stage. This representation enables parallel reasoning decoding (Figure 1). We use the language model directly as candidate classifier, without any additional head, to score each reasoning candidate by its length-normalized likelihood conditioned on the current context. This leverages the language understanding capability of the model to match the context to the most suitable reasoning. Since all candidate tokens are pre-specified, teacher forcing computes token likelihoods in parallel within each reasoning candidate, and candidates are also scored concurrently sharing the same KV cache. The model then samples reasoning candidate based on its score, and the harness inserts the selected reasoning into the model context as natural-language guidance for the next action. We evaluate SSR across seven multimodal search benchmarks. Our 4B SSR with GRPO model achieves an average success rate of 61.37%, matching the performance of leading trained 4B search agents (61.25%). Across GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), GSPO (Zheng et al., 2025b), SAPO (Gao et al., 2025), and SFT, the SSR agents achieve comparable task performance while significantly reducing model inference latency compared to the freeform reasoning counterpart. Against four representative efficient reasoning baselines, SSR achieves higher success rate, lower model inference time, and more consistent latency. In summary, our contributions are three-fold: Reasoning by selection rather than generation. We introduce Selection-based Structured Reasoning (SSR), which replaces freeform reasoning with selection among reusable natural language candidates conditioned on the current context. Parallel reasoning decoding. We use the language model itself to score reasoning candidates by their length-normalized likelihoods. This approach requires neither an additional classification head nor an SFT warm start. Teacher forcing enables parallel scoring across all tokens within and between candidates, eliminating autoregressive generation of reasoning traces. Competitive performance with substantial efficiency gains. Across GRPO, GSPO, SAPO, and SFT, our 4B agents maintain competitive performance while reducing mean reasoning latency per turn by over 90% and mean model latency per question by 2854%.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: 2.1 MULTIMODAL SEARCH AGENTS Prior work trained multimodal agents to interleave perception, retrieval, and tool use. In multimodal search, MMSearch-R1 (Wu et al., 2025) and DeepMMSearch-R1 (Narayan et al., 2025) trained models to use text and image search, while Visual-ARFT (Liu et al., 2025) and DeepEyes (Zheng et al., 2026) added image operations such as cropping and zooming. DeepEyesV2 (Hong et al., 2026) combined image operations with code execution and web search. SenseNova-MARS (Chng et al., 2025), TAPO (Dong et al., 2026), and WebWatcher (Geng et al., 2025) investigated multi-turn reinforcement learning, tool-aware credit assignment, and deep-research behavior. More recent systems extended the scale and supervision of this recipe: VSearcher trained long-horizon search over text, 2 images, and webpages (Zhang et al., 2026), while ProMMSearchAgent introduced process-oriented rewards in static sandbox before transfer to live search (Yan et al., 2026). These approaches focused on training-data mixtures, gradient routing, and credit assignment for performance improvements, while we explore an orthogonal direction that improves inference efficiency.

sections.title: 2.2 EFFICIENT REASONING FOR MLLM AGENTS
sections.content: Efficient-reasoning methods controlled model deliberation through token budgets, early stopping, compressed chains of thought, or adaptive test-time computation (Han et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025; Sui et al., 2025). Agentic settings add another resource axis: the model must decide not only how long to think, but also whether to spend the next unit of budget on retrieval, interaction, or answer commitment. Inference-time budget control for search agents explicitly modeled this trade-off (Fang et al., 2026). Closest to our efficiency goal, HyperEyes (Li et al., 2026) treated inference efficiency as first-class training objective: it dispatched multiple grounded queries concurrently within round and rewarded trajectories that avoided superfluous tool calls, reducing the number of interaction rounds, whereas we reduce the cost of the reasoning span within each round. Grammar-constrained decoding enforced admissible output forms (Geng et al., 2023), with engines such as XGrammar reducing the cost of constraint checking (Dong et al., 2025). SSR instead scores complete candidates in parallel and directly supplies the selected text as the reasoning trace. 2.3 REUSABLE REASONING AND AGENT SKILLS Prior work explored reusable knowledge through thought templates (Yang et al., 2024), contextaware guidelines (Fu et al., 2024), reasoning memories (Ouyang et al., 2026), and task workflows (Wang et al., 2025). Given library of reasoning candidates, SSR directly uses the acting MLLMs internal semantic knowledge to select among them through context-conditioned likelihoods, without any auxiliary knowledge-management or retrieval system. Trajectory-level approaches such as StraTA (Xue et al., 2026) generated strategy from the initial task state and kept that strategy fixed throughout the interaction. SSR instead selects reasoning candidate at every turn based on the updated interaction history, allowing new observations to change the guidance for subsequent actions. Programmatic approaches (Wang et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2025a) encoded reusable skills as fixed, executable programs. An SSR candidate instead supplies natural-language guidance that biases action generation without prescribing executable control flow. This leaves concrete queries, tool arguments, and answers flexible, allowing the same reasoning candidate to support different actions across contexts without modifying the candidate itself.

sections.title: 3 SELECTION-BASED STRUCTURED REASONING
sections.content: 3.1 OVERVIEW We introduce Selection-based Structured Reasoning (SSR), which replaces freeform reasoning in ReAct agents (Yao et al., 2022) with selection among reusable reasoning candidates. At turn t, the interaction history of an agent is ht = [x, z0, a0, o0, . . . , zt1, at1, ot1], where is the initial user request, zi is reasoning trace, ai is an action, and oi is the observation returned by an external tool. tool call extends the history with new observation, while final answer terminates the trajectory. Conventionally, an MLLM with distribution pθ generates freeform reasoning trace zt pθ( ht) before generating the action at pθ( ht, zt). Since zt is unconstrained naturallanguage text, its tokens must be decoded autoregressively, resulting in substantial inference latency. To eliminate this sequential decoding cost, SSR selects zt from reusable natural-language candidates conditioned on ht, instead of generating it token by token (Figure 2). SSR contains reasoning library = {r1, . . . , rN }, which consists of short natural-language candidates. Each candidate is reusable reasoning trace that describes what information is available or missing in the current context and what step to take next. Parallel reasoning decoding uses the language model itself to score the full text of each candidate conditioned on ht and select one as zt. Since all candidate texts are specified in advance, their token likelihoods can be computed with teacher-forced prefill and different candidates can be scored in parallel. The selected reasoning is then inserted into the context to guide instance-specific action generation, such as search query, crop location, or final answer. 3 Figure 2: Overview of Selection-based Structured Reasoning. Freeform agents generate tokenby-token reasoning before each action. SSR instead selects from library of reusable naturallanguage reasoning candidates. Parallel reasoning decoding scores every token in each candidate using teacher-forced prefill, and the selected candidate guides context-specific action generation. This formulation leverages the semantics prior in the language decoder for reasoning selection, and makes use of the natural-language guidance for the action generation. 3.2 PARALLEL REASONING DECODING Scoring and selection. sections.title: 4.1 SETUP
sections.content: Datasets. Following prior work (Chng et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2026), we use VisualProbe (Lai et al., 2026), DeepEyes (Zheng et al., 2026), and FVQA-train (Wu et al., 2025) for training, and use MMSearch (Jiang et al., 2024), HR-MMSearch (Chng et al., 2025), FVQA-test (Wu et al., 2025), InfoSeek (Chen et al., 2023), SimpleVQA (Cheng et al., 2025), LiveVQA (Fu et al., 2025), and MAT-Search (Liu et al., 2025) for evaluation. Appendix details the datasets used. Implementation details. We use the 2B/4B Qwen3-VL (Qwen Team, 2025) models for our experiments. Following the aforementioned prior work, we use the same tool harness with reverse-image search, text search, and image cropping, as well as the same LLM-as-judge for evaluation. Our reasoning library contains six manually written reasoning candidates shared across benchmarks (details in Appendix E): (1) doing an image search to identify the entity when unsure, (2) looking up specific information through text search, (3) zooming into specific part of the image for targeted inspection, (4) answering the question from the gathered evidence, (5) answering the question based on the image, and (6) answering with general knowledge. Each of them covers general case that the search agent may encounter. Unless otherwise noted, we train each RL model in single stage for one epoch with learning rate of 105 using outcome and format rewards. For simplicity, we set λSFT reason = 1 and β = 103. Appendix contains additional implementation details. reason = γRL Evaluation metrics. We report success rate on all seven multimodal search benchmarks and inference efficiency. For latency profiling, we sample 100 questions per benchmark and measure per-turn reasoning latency (time to produce the reasoning trace) and per-question model latency (prefill, reasoning, action generation, and other model inference over the full trajectory). We report mean and 95th-percentile latency. Environment-side processing, including tool execution and LLM-as-judge evaluation, is excluded as it introduces excessive model-independent variations. We also report effective reasoning throughput, computed as the total number of reasoning tokens processed divided by the total reasoning time. For SSR, this counts all candidate tokens being scored in parallel. For autoregressive generation, it counts the tokens in the generated reasoning trace. We run the profiling on an NVIDIA H100 GPU with an offline SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024) inference engine. 4.2 SSR ACHIEVES COMPETITIVE TASK PERFORMANCE We first compare SSR with the state-of-the-art multimodal search agents. Table 1 shows that the 4B SSR model reaches 61.37% average success rate, comparable to the best 4B SOTA model TAPO with GSPO at 61.25% and outperforms 4B MMSearch-R1 and SenseNova-MARS baselines. We implement the efficiency baselines on the GRPO-freeform pipeline for fair comparison and report the results in Table 3. Higher success rate with lower inference latency. SSR achieves the highest success rate and delivers approximately 7 or greater speedup in reasoning on all baselines. The gains extend to question-level: mean model latency is around 2.5s, approximately 30% lower than Sketch-ofThought, the fastest baseline on this metric. These results show that parallel reasoning decoding is more effective than reasoning-compression methods at reducing latency while maintaining high success rate. The speed advantage is even larger at the 95th percentile. SSR has p95 reasoning time of 0.071s, 10 ms above its mean, whereas the p95 latency for the baselines range from 0.798 to 1.892s. The tight mean-to-p95 gap indicates consistent reasoning latency in SSR, matching the predictable computation of scoring all candidates in parallel as opposed to freeform generation with varying lengths. At the question level, p95 latency is 4.6s, about 30% reduction from the 6.6s of the fastest baseline. 4.5 COMPARISON BETWEEN DIFFERENT REASONING METHODS We ablate the generation methods and compare different ways to select reasoning from the library. Table 4 compares full-reasoning-text selection, index-only selection, and autoregressive reasoning generation. These variants distinguish the effects of the reasoning selection mechanism in SSR. Reasoning representation for candidate selection. The index-only variant applies Eq. 1 to the index of each candidate (e.g., [1]) rather than its full text, then relies on the harness to inject the selected candidate before action generation. Both variants supply the same structured reasoning to the action generation, but index-only scoring selects without access to the semantics of the reasoning tokens. This change lowers average success by 3.9%, affecting all seven benchmarks. This comparison highlights the value of reasoning-candidate semantics for better context-dependent selection. 8 Figure 3: Reasoning library size. Average success rate increases as the library size grows. Figure 4: Reasoning selection distribution across benchmarks. The same checkpoint exhibits different reasoning-selection distributions across benchmarks. Selection vs. autoregressive generation. Autoregressive decoding can also generate the specified reasoning candidate when the model is trained to use the library entries. With an SFT warm start followed by RL with format reward, the 4B model reproduces reasoning-library entries and achieves average success comparable to parallel reasoning decoding. However, without SFT, specifying in the prompt and applying format reward during RL cannot enforce using only the reasoning candidates from the library, and the model instead generates freeform reasoning. Thus, the autoregressive variant must learn to conform to the reasoning library, whereas our reasoning selection enforces this interface directly. Additionally, parallel full-text scoring further removes the sequential generation of the selected reasoning candidate, combining effective reasoning with lower decoding latency. 4.6 REASONING LIBRARY SIZE AND SELECTION DISTRIBUTION Effect of library size. Figure 3 compares libraries with one, two, four, and six entries, ranging from single generic candidate, am helpful assistant, to six more specific reasoning candidates. Success rate across seven benchmarks increases monotonically from 37.24% to 61.37%, showing that more detailed, granular reasoning candidates better guide learning for action generation. The 17.27 percentage point gain from one generic candidate to two candidates, answer or tool call, highlights the value of meaningful reasoning choices even in small library. Reasoning selection distribution. Figure 4 shows that the same model yields different distributions of reasoning selection across different benchmarks. Specifically, the simplest SimpleVQA has the highest selection rate for Answer from image and the lowest for Look up fact and the highresolution image centric HR-MMSearch has the highest selection rate for Examine image detail. These distribution differences suggest that SSR adapts its choices to question-specific information needs despite using shared library. These reasoning choices are reflected in action generation: in 99.9% of turns, the generated action type matches the expected action type of the selected candidate. The agent is indeed demonstrating behaviors that match the charasteristics of different benchmarks.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented Selection-based Structured Reasoning (SSR), which reformulates reasoning in small multimodal search agents as selection rather than open-ended generation. SSR captures recurring high-level reasoning as reusable natural-language candidates and selects among them based on their likelihoods under the current context. Pre-specified candidates enable teacher-forced parallel scoring within and across candidates, eliminating token-by-token reasoning generation. Across seven multimodal search benchmarks, SSR achieves competitive task performance while reducing per-turn reasoning latency by over 90% and total per-question model inference latency by 28-54%. More broadly, our results suggest that small search agents may not need to reason over the full language space at every step, and that organizing recurring reasoning into compact, reusable space can enable more efficient multimodal agents.

sections.content: D.1 TRAINING DATASETS We use the 3,859-example training mixture from TAPO/SenseNova-MARS (Dong et al., 2026; Chng et al., 2025), with the subset sizes and accuracy rewards shown in Table 5. It trains the agent to identify when image or text retrieval is needed. DeepEyes-4K. Our training mixture includes both multiple-choice (MCQ) and non-MCQ subsets. VisualProbe-train. We use the benchmark versions distributed in the SenseNova evaluation collection (Chng et al., 2025). MMSearch (Jiang et al., 2024) contains 300 manually collected questions spanning 14 subfields, of which 171 are accompanied by an image; its News area covers events from May to August 2024, testing the models ability to ground visual observations in up-to-date factual knowledge. We follow the standard split of 171 questions used for system-level evaluation. HR-MMSearch (Chng et al., 2025) is knowledge-intensive benchmark comprising 305 questions paired with high-resolution (4K) images sourced from international news agencies (2025 events), spanning eight topical domains. Approximately 60% of questions are classified as hard, requiring three or more tool invocations to answer correctly. FVQA-test (Wu et al., 2025) is curated 1,800-sample test set consisting of three equal-sized subsets: FVQA-auto-vc (600 automatically constructed samples, each manually checked for correctness and disjoint from the training set), InfoSeek Human Split (600 samples with manually corrected annotations), and an expert-annotated subset (600 samples). InfoSeek (Chen et al., 2023) is visual question answering dataset for information-seeking questions that cannot be answered through commonsense reasoning alone. It is built on visual entity recognition and grounded in Wikidata, targeting fine-grained factual attributes that models do not reliably surface without retrieval. We sample 2,000 instances from its test split. SimpleVQA (Cheng et al., 2025) focuses on factual accuracy, combining post-2023 VQA instances with expert-curated image-question pairs across 1,013 English samples. LiveVQA (Fu et al., 2025) aggregates 3,602 image-question pairs from major news outlets, including CNN and BBC, spanning 14 thematic categories, and emphasizes temporal reasoning over recently published content. MAT-Search (Liu et al., 2025) is manually crafted and human-verified benchmark of 150 examples designed to evaluate agentic multimodal reasoning, requiring models to handle composite 19 multi-hop queries, retrieve external information, and invoke tools effectively across varying reasoning depths.

sections.title: F TRAINING DETAILS
sections.content: Reference recipe and our adaptation. We adapt the multimodal-search setup of TAPO (Dong et al., 2026). The agent is trained directly with RL, without an SFT warm-up, using VeRL, global batch size of 64, learning rate 1 105, and 8 rollouts per GRPO group. Each trajectory permits at most 10 interaction rounds during training, 8,192 generated tokens per round, and 32,768 tokens across the full trajectory. If it exceeds any of these, it will be marked as incorrect. Text retrieval during training uses local Wikipedia retrieval index to reduce cost and evaluation uses web search through Serp API. Action space. The agent can choose among three information-acquisition tools and terminal answer: (i) image search tool, which performs reverse-image search on the question image and returns image captions; (ii) text search tool(query), which performs query-specified (iii) image zoom in tool(bbox), search and returns Qwen3-32B-generated summary; which crops bounding box and returns the resulting image patch; and (iv) terminal <answer> action. At every non-terminal turn, the base protocol expects thinking block followed by exactly one <tool call> conforming to the JSON schema; SSR supplies the thinking block through candidate selection while retaining the same tool-call schema. Reward. For RL, we use combination of accuracy reward and format reward. rfinal = raccuracy + 0.5rformat (20) Non-multiple-choice questions are judged by Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct with greedy decoding and temperature zero given the image, question, ground truth, and the final answer generated by the model. Multiple-choice questions use exact match. Format reward is model-dependent: all conditions have to generate valid <think> delimiters and correct tool call format; SSR models (including the index-only variant) additionally have to use the expected tool of each reasoning that they select for full format reward, otherwise they only get partial format reward for the correct tool call 20 format; the autoregressive structured reasoning model gets the format reward only if it generates reasoning in the library with exact match. REASONING COMPARISON: NO THINKING, FREEFORM, AND SSR We compare no thinking, freeform reasoning, and SSR (ours) under GRPO with the Qwen3-VL-4B backbone. Figure 5: Success rate (%) of the three reasoning types on the multimodal search benchmarks. Aggregate comparison. Figure 5 compares no thinking, freeform reasoning, and SSR under GRPO. The unweighted mean success rate across the seven benchmarks is 58.91%, 58.65%, and 61.37%, respectively. SSR therefore improves the benchmark mean by 2.47 percentage points over no thinking and 2.72 points over freeform reasoning. Freeform reasoning is 0.26 points below no thinking on this aggregate, so generating freeform reasoning trace does not by itself consistently improve task performance in this comparison. Consistent gains over no thinking. SSR outperforms no thinking on all seven benchmarks (7/7), with gains ranging from 0.99 to 7.34 percentage points. In contrast, freeform reasoning improves over no thinking on only two of seven benchmarks with the same Qwen3-VL-4B backbone under GRPO. SSR improves over no thinking across all seven benchmarks whereas freeform does not outperform no thinking on all of the benchmarks. SSR also exceeds freeform reasoning on five of seven benchmarks, with HR-MMSearch and MAT-Search favoring freeform reasoning.
